label: Tube implosion risk
summary: A CRT picture tube holds a strong vacuum behind thick glass. A crack, a knock to the thin neck, or a hard blow to the face can make it implode and throw glass. The tube also stores a high-voltage charge on its anode.
signs: Deep, heavy TVs and computer monitors, mostly made before about 2010
A thin glass neck at the back of the tube with a socket on the end
A rubber suction cup on the side of the tube with a thick lead going to it: the anode connection
Old oscilloscopes, arcade machines and rear-projection TVs
do: Leave the tube in one piece unless you have a real use for what's around it
Lift by the cabinet or the tube's mounting ears, never the neck
Set the set face-down on a blanket to work on it

Discharge the anode before touching anything near the tube: slide an insulated probe or long screwdriver, wired to the tube's metal ground strap, under the suction cup; do it again before each touch, as the tube can recharge itself
Keep people and pets clear while you work
dont: Don't knock, lever against or put weight on the neck
Don't drop it, or carry a big one alone
Don't smash a tube to get rid of it
Don't try to let the vacuum out yourself
Don't remove or loosen the metal band around the front of the tube: it holds the glass together
firstAid: Glass in an eye: don't rub. Rinse out loose specks with clean water; if glass is stuck in the eye or the eye is cut, don't rinse or pull it out: tape a paper cup over it without pressing and get medical help
Cuts: press firmly with a clean pad for 10 minutes; deep or gaping cuts need medical care
Shock from the anode: follow the first aid for stored high voltage
